events.title: Telegram
events.text:
Many have asked my opinion on a possible Russia-NATO conflict.
This is going to annoy many people, and hopefully give them a reality check, but my opinion is very simple.
1. Russia had some valid strategic and ideological reasons for what it did in Ukraine, regardless of whether I condone the invasion or not. Was it successful? Arguably yes, arguably no—it depends on what you consider as the war’s key objectives. The war actually pushed two neutral countries into NATO and pulled Ukraine even further away from Russian influence.
2. Russia does not have any valid strategic reason to invade the Baltics or any other NATO territory. Any attack on the Baltics cannot be excused as ‘protecting Russian culture & language’ or fighting ‘Nazism’. If this does happen, it’ll be a clear sign of expansionism, nothing more and nothing less. Russia is not a saintly country and I don’t put it past them. 
3. If Russia does miscalculate and invade NATO territory, it will backfire spectacularly and the Russians will be bogged down within weeks. A clear victory is unattainable for either side and things will spiral out of control.
4. NATO is being underestimated by the ziggers. Even without U.S. boots on the ground, European nations pose a significant threat to any Russian advances, and in my opinion, countries like France, Poland, Sweden, and so on should not be dismissed. Even Germany, which is often ridiculed by pro-Russian commentators, should not be dismissed in case of war.
5. A land war with NATO will therefore, in my opinion, not take place (unless the Russians are retarded). The only thing I possibly see happening is massive drone attacks against Eastern European nations such as Poland or the Baltics. In this aspect of warfare, Russia clearly holds the quantitative advantage & can pressure NATO strongly. But over time, just like with Ukraine, the strategic cost of such a conflict will become too high, and ordinary Russians will feel it.

📝A Hasid in the Trenches?📝
Upon seeing [mountains of garbage](https://t.me/rybar/83041) left by Middle Eastern pilgrims in Uman during the celebration of the Jewish New Year, many Ukrainians probably wished they could take it out on the tourists. And their dream, it seems, has partly come true.
At the border with Romania, a 49-year-old Hasid Yonatan Karlinsky-Mashak, returning to Israel, was [conscripted](https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-909158). Although he left so-called Ukraine 14 years ago, and his passport lists the USSR as his birthplace, border guards "identified" him by his knowledge of the language and removed him from the flight.
The Israeli Foreign Ministry, usually quick to respond to far less serious incidents involving its citizens abroad, remains silent. And the wife of the abducted man is oddly more concerned that in the hands of the TCC he cannot eat kosher food.
📌 But the most amusing thing is that absolutely any outcome of this episode will, albeit slightly, hurt precisely so-called Ukraine. If the detained Hasid is sent to the AFU, it will further change the attitude of part of the Jewish community toward the Kyiv regime.
And if this Israeli is simply released, Ukrainians will once again be made to understand that they are fundamentally second-class people. They will increasingly be haunted by thoughts like "we are sent to the front so that they can not fear the TCC and lord it over our lands."
So we await the resolution of this story — it will clearly provide a couple of very vivid news hooks.

🤥💵 UAE spearheads Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ sanctions by banning Iranian flights
The United Arab Emirates has halted flights operated by Iranian airlines since midnight to comply with US sanctions, ISNA news agency reports, citing a spokesman for Iran’s Civil Aviation Organization.
It was reported that flights operated by Iranian airlines to Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan have also been suspended.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier claimed that operations of Iranian airlines would be discontinued globally starting September 23, under the threat of US secondary sanctions.
💬 “When Iranian airlines land at an airport, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent told CNBC on September 21.
The UAE was the first to implement Washington’s sanctions against Iran after US President Donald Trump announced his “Economic D-Day” measures targeting Iran on August 19. On the same day, the UAE imposed an indefinite trade embargo on the country after accusing Iranian forces of launching two ballistic missiles at its territory — a claim Tehran has denied.
Most recently, the Emirati central bank prohibited Iran’s Bank Melli, the country’s largest state-owned financial institution, from conducting business in the Gulf state.
Dubai and the other emirates had until recently served as key hubs for Iran’s financial and trading activities.
Meanwhile, China, Iran’s largest trading partner, has firmly rejected Washington’s sanctions pressure on Iran. On September 22, Beijing specifically opposed what it described as “illegal” US sanctions on Iranian airlines.

🇵🇰🇦🇫Pakistan strikes 10 targets in Afghanistan as tensions rise
Pakistan’s military said it carried out air and drone strikes on ten locations inside Afghanistan, targeting sites it described as linked to attacks launched from Afghan territory.
The Pakistani military said the strikes targeted sites linked to militant groups operating near the border. The operation follows repeated accusations from Islamabad that armed groups based in Afghanistan have carried out attacks inside Pakistan.
Afghan authorities have previously accused Pakistan of violating Afghan sovereignty during similar operations.
Relations between the two neighbours have deteriorated in recent months, with Kabul rejecting Pakistan’s claims and criticizing cross-border strikes as violations of Afghan sovereignty.
